steps.title: Definition
steps.body: Synthesis means combining information from different sources to create a summary. You draw together ideas from both texts to show common themes or differences.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.body: Read both texts and identify the key information Step 2: Decide what each text says about the topic Step 3: Find similarities and/or differences Step 4: Write in your own words, using brief quotations Step 5: Organise logically - group related points

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: In synthesis questions, don't analyse language devices. Focus on summarising what each text says about the topic.

steps.title: Examiner's Tip
steps.body: This is NOT a language analysis question. Focus on what each text SAYS - the content and ideas. Use your own words and keep quotations brief. Spend about 10 minutes on this question.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: What is the main difference between synthesis and comparison? | Should you analyse language devices in a synthesis question? | How should you use quotations in synthesis?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Synthesis focuses on WHAT texts say (content); comparison focuses on HOW they convey meaning (methods). | No - synthesis is about summarising content, not analysing language. | Keep them brief and use them as evidence to support your summary points.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Focus on content, not language analysis Use evidence from both texts equally Write in your own words where possible Use synthesis sentence starters Don't write too much - 8 marks needs a concise response Group related points logically Answer the specific question focus
